procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 25, 1967, of the Mysore High Court dismissing Writ Petitions Nos. 741, 973, 974, and 975 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Town Municipal Council, Athani, filed four writ petitions (Nos. 741, 973, 974, and 975 of 1966) in the Mysore High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution, challenging the decision of the Labour Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions by a common order dated August 25, 1967.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Town Municipal Council, Athani, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the common judgment of the Mysore High Court dismissing the four writ petitions. The Civil Appeals Nos. 170, 171, 172, and 173 of 1968 are directed against the order governing Writ Petitions Nos. 741/1966, 973/1966, 974/1966, and 975/1966 respectively.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the Labour Court to entertain applications under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is excluded because the claims could have been made under Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.

facts: Workmen filed applications under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (IDA) to claim payment for overtime and work done on weekly off-days.
The employer (appellant) challenged the Labour Court's jurisdiction, arguing that the claims should have been made under Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 (MWA).
In this specific case, there was no dispute between the employer and the workmen regarding the *rates* of pay for overtime or off-day work.
law: The Supreme Court interpreted the scope of Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act.
It held that the MWA is primarily concerned with the *fixing of rates* (minimum wages, overtime, etc.) and is not intended for the general enforcement of wage payments.
A remedy under Section 20(1) of the MWA is available only when there is a dispute about the applicable rates of pay.
application: The Court applied its interpretation of the law to the facts of the case.
Since the employer did not dispute the rates of pay claimed by the workmen, the Court found that the claims did not fall under the scope of Section 20(1) of the MWA.
Therefore, the workmen could not have sought a remedy under the Minimum Wages Act in this instance.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the employer's argument. It concluded that because the workmen's claims could not have been made under the Minimum Wages Act (as there was no dispute about the rates), the question of the MWA excluding the Labour Court's jurisdiction under the Industrial Disputes Act did not arise. The Labour Court was, therefore, competent to hear the applications under Section 33C(2) of the IDA.

issue.issue_text: Whether the question of limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, could be allowed to be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court, even though it was not raised in the Labour Court or the High Court.

facts: The appellant sought to raise the issue that the claims were time-barred under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
This specific issue of limitation under Article 137 was not raised in the Labour Court or the High Court.
Before the final hearing in the Supreme Court, the appellant filed a written application seeking permission to raise this new point.
The respondents (the workmen) were served notice of this application and were aware that the appellant intended to argue this point.
law: The Supreme Court held that a question of limitation is a "pure question of law."
Such a question raises a "plea of want of jurisdiction," meaning it challenges the court's authority to hear the case.
application: The Court reasoned that since the issue of limitation was a pure question of law, it could be raised at any stage, including for the first time in the Supreme Court.
A key condition was that the question could be decided based on the facts already on the record, without needing new evidence.
The Court also noted that the respondents were not unfairly surprised, as they had received sufficient notice through the appellant's formal application to raise the new point.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's request and allowed the question of limitation to be raised for the first time. It did so because the issue was a pure question of law concerning jurisdiction that could be decided on the existing record, and the respondents had been given fair notice of the new argument.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the Labour Court to entertain applications under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is excluded because the claims could have been made under Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948.
appellant_arguments: The jurisdiction of the Labour Court to handle claims under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act is barred because the same relief could have been sought by the workmen under Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's arguments on this issue, but their position, which the court upheld, was that the Labour Court's jurisdiction was not barred.

cases.case_name: Sha Mulchand & Co. Ltd. (In Liquidation) v. Jawahar Mills Ltd.
cases.principle: The long-standing judicial interpretation that Article 181 of the 1908 Limitation Act applied only to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure was so established that it was as if the words 'under the Code' were written into the article itself, and this established meaning was not altered by subsequent amendments to other articles in the schedule.

cases.case_name: Bombay Gas Co. Ltd. v. Gopal Bhiva and Others
cases.principle: Affirming the principle from Sha Mulchand, it held that Article 181 of the 1908 Limitation Act, being confined to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure, could not be invoked for applications under s. 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The residuary article for applications in the Limitation Act, 1963 (Article 137), is confined to applications made under the Code of Civil Procedure and does not extend to applications made under other statutes, such as an application under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act.
obiter: A long-standing judicial construction of a statute is not automatically altered by a subsequent amendment that merely removes the original reason for that construction.

The jurisdiction of the Authority under Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act is for deciding claims relating to disputes over the rates of wages and is not attracted where there is no dispute as to the rates and the only question is the enforcement of payment.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The jurisdiction of the Labour Court under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act is not excluded by the remedy available under Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act. The latter provision is intended to address disputes over the rates of wages fixed under the Act, not for the simple enforcement of payment of amounts where the rates themselves are not in dispute. As the workmen's claims did not involve a dispute over rates, the remedy under the Minimum Wages Act was not available to them, and therefore, the Labour Court's jurisdiction was not barred.
legal_tests_applied: A new point of law can be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court if it is a pure question of law that raises a plea of want of jurisdiction, can be decided on the basis of the facts already on record, and the opposing party has been given sufficient notice.

The jurisdiction of a specialized authority under a statute (like the Minimum Wages Act) is determined by the primary purpose of the provision, not by its incidental powers. The power to direct payment under Section 20(3) of the Minimum Wages Act is incidental to the primary purpose of ensuring compliance with the wage rates fixed under that Act.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's primary argument failed because the Court determined that Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act does not cover all claims for minimum wages. Its purpose is to ensure compliance with the rates fixed under the Act, which applies when there is a dispute about the applicable rate.

In this case, there was no dispute between the parties regarding the rates for minimum wages, overtime, or payment for days of rest. Therefore, the remedy under Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act was not available to the workmen.

Since the remedy under the Minimum Wages Act was not applicable to the facts of the case, the question of it barring the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act did not arise.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position on the jurisdictional issue was upheld because the Court found that the Labour Court was the appropriate forum for their claims. The claims were for the enforcement of payment of an amount due, where the rate of payment was not in dispute, fitting within the scope of Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act.

The Court accepted that the power of the Authority under Section 20(1) of the Minimum Wages Act is not for the general enforcement of payments but specifically for ensuring compliance with the wage rates fixed under that Act, a situation not present in this case.
policy_considerations: The Court's interpretation harmonises the provisions of the Minimum Wages Act with the provisions of the Payment of Wages Act, which already existed when the Minimum Wages Act was passed.

Allowing a pure question of law concerning jurisdiction (like limitation) to be raised for the first time at the Supreme Court level upholds the principle that courts should not act without jurisdiction, provided that the question can be decided on existing facts and the opposing party is given sufficient notice through a formal application.
